q: A railway hospital works out the cost of the service rendered by it for a period per patient-day. The method of costing it is applying is:

options.B: Job costing
options.C: Contract costing
options.D: Batch costing

q: In the operating costing of a transport undertaking, which of the following is a running charge?

options.A: The annual licence fee of the vehicle
options.B: The insurance premium of the vehicle
options.C: Diesel fuel consumed by the vehicle in running
options.D: The rent of the garage where the vehicle is housed

q: In operating costing, the operating costs of a service undertaking are commonly collected under the three heads of:

options.A: Prime cost, works cost and cost of production
options.B: Material cost, labour cost and direct expenses
options.C: Standing charges, maintenance charges and running charges
options.D: Fixed cost, variable cost and semi-variable cost

q: The total operating cost of a passenger service for a period is Rs 31,50,000 and the service rendered during the period is 90,00,000 passenger-kilometres. The operating cost per passenger-kilometre is:

The standing charges of a passenger transport service remain much the same whether the vehicles run full or partly empty. If the average occupancy of the service falls, its operating cost per passenger-kilometre will:

options.A: Rise, because the standing charges are then spread over a smaller number of passenger-kilometres
options.B: Fall, because fewer passengers are carried during the period
options.C: Remain exactly the same in all circumstances
options.D: Become equal to the fare charged per passenger-kilometre

q: Operating costing differs from job costing in that, under operating costing, costs are collected:

options.A: Only when the undertaking is first set up
options.B: Against each customer's order as and when it is completed
options.C: Only for capital works executed by the undertaking
options.D: For a period of time, such as a month, and are then related to the units of service rendered during that period

q: In the costing of joint products, the split-off point is the point at which:

options.A: The joint products are finally sold to the customers
options.B: Further processing of every joint product is completed
options.C: The products arising from the common process become separately identifiable as distinct products
options.D: The joint costs of the process are first incurred

q: A recognised feature of apportioning joint costs among joint products on the basis of their sales values is that:

options.A: Every joint product is charged with exactly the same total amount of joint cost
options.B: No joint cost at all is charged to the product with the lowest sales value
options.C: The joint cost is apportioned in proportion to the weight of each product alone
options.D: All the joint products show the same overall percentage of gross margin on their sales values

q: Under the average unit cost method of apportioning joint costs, the joint cost borne by each joint product is worked out by:

options.A: Dividing the total joint cost by the total number of units of all the joint products, to get an average cost per unit which is applied to the units of each product
options.B: Charging the whole joint cost to the product with the highest sales value
options.C: Apportioning the joint cost in the ratio of the further processing costs of the products
options.D: Deducting the sales value of the by-products from the joint cost first

q: Where a by-product recovered in a process is of very small value and has no regular use, a commonly followed treatment of the amount realised from its sale is to:

options.A: Add it to the joint cost of the process
options.B: Charge it to the main product as an additional cost
options.C: Credit it to the general Profit and Loss Account as a miscellaneous income, the main product bearing the whole cost of the process
options.D: Carry it forward indefinitely as a stock of the process

q: A joint cost of Rs 90,000 is to be apportioned between joint products A and B on the basis of the physical quantity of output. A gives an output of 2,000 kg and B gives an output of 1,000 kg. The share of joint cost borne by product A is:

A joint cost of Rs 4,20,000 is to be apportioned between joint products A and B on the basis of their net realisable values. A can be sold for Rs 6,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 1,20,000, and B can be sold for Rs 4,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 40,000. The share of joint cost borne by product A is:

The total cost of a process is Rs 3,30,000, from which 11,000 units of the main product are obtained. A by-product recovered in the process is sold for Rs 33,000 and the amount is credited to the process account. The cost per unit of the main product is:

options.B: Rs 30
options.C: Rs 33
options.D: Rs 24

q: The main purpose served by charging the output of a process to the next process at a price which includes a margin of profit is that:

options.A: The total profit of the factory as a whole is increased by the internal transfers
options.B: No stock reserve is ever needed for the closing stocks of the processes
options.C: Each process can be judged as a separate profit centre and its efficiency compared with the price at which its output could be bought from the market
options.D: The closing stock of the factory can be shown in the balance sheet at the transfer price

q: The output of a process is transferred to the next process at cost plus 25% on cost. The closing stock of the receiving process, valued at the transfer price, is Rs 80,000. The unrealised profit contained in this stock, for which a stock reserve is required, is:

Funds locked up in current assets are not consumed once for all; as stock is sold and debtors are realised, the funds are released and become available again for buying fresh stock. This feature of working capital is described as its:

options.B: Depreciation over a period of time
options.C: Revolving or circulating character, the same funds moving again and again through stock, debtors and cash
options.D: Character of a long-term investment

q: The current assets of an enterprise are Rs 7,40,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 3,20,000. Its net working capital is:
The current assets of an enterprise are Rs 9,60,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 4,00,000. Its current ratio is:

The current assets of an enterprise are Rs 11,00,000, comprising stock of Rs 4,50,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 50,000, the balance being liquid assets. Its current liabilities are Rs 3,00,000. Its quick (acid-test) ratio is:

An enterprise holds stock of Rs 3,20,000, debtors of Rs 2,40,000, short-term investments of Rs 60,000 and cash and bank balances of Rs 65,000, and has no other current assets. Its gross working capital is:

Over and above the minimum level of working capital maintained throughout the year, a sugar mill needs extra funds for a few months when it buys cane heavily in the crushing season and builds up its stock. This extra requirement is its:

options.A: Temporary (fluctuating) working capital, needed only for the seasonal peak and repaid when the season ends
options.B: Permanent working capital, needed throughout the year
options.C: Fixed capital, invested in plant and machinery
options.D: Reserve capital, kept for use in an emergency only

q: A firm finances even a part of its seasonal needs from long-term funds and keeps the surplus so raised parked in short-term securities during the slack season. The working capital financing approach followed by the firm is the:

options.B: Matching approach
options.C: Hedging approach
options.D: Conservative approach

q: Two units make the same product. In one unit each batch remains in process for three weeks, while in the other it remains in process for only one week, all other conditions being the same. The unit with the longer process will generally require:

options.A: Less working capital, because its work-in-progress turns over faster
options.B: More working capital, because its funds remain locked up in work-in-progress for a longer time before the finished product can be sold
options.C: Exactly the same working capital as the other unit
options.D: No working capital at all, because the process is continuous

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 2/10, net 30, that is, a cash discount of 2 per cent for payment within 10 days and the full amount payable in 30 days. The approximate annualised cost of not taking the cash discount, reckoning a year of 365 days, is:
The safety stock of a material is held by an enterprise primarily in order to:

options.A: Guard against a stock-out and stoppage of production when consumption rises unexpectedly or fresh supplies are delayed beyond the normal lead time
options.B: Take advantage of a fall in the market price of the material
options.C: Earn a profit by reselling the material to other firms
options.D: Show a higher value of stock in the balance sheet

q: The main purpose of offering a cash discount to customers for payment well before the due date is to:

options.A: Increase the selling price of the goods
options.B: Reduce the cost of manufacturing the goods
options.C: Postpone the collection of dues from the customers
options.D: Accelerate the collection of receivables and so reduce the funds blocked in debtors and the risk of bad debts

q: In fixing the minimum cash balance that an enterprise should keep, the balance is in substance struck between:

options.A: The dividend expected by the shareholders and the interest payable to the bank
options.B: The risk and cost of running short of cash for meeting payments, and the opportunity cost of keeping idle cash that could otherwise be put to earning use
options.C: The cash in hand and the cash at bank of the enterprise
options.D: The receipts of the current month and the payments of the next month

q: In a manufacturing enterprise, raw materials are held for 28 days, the production process takes 14 days, finished goods are held for 18 days and debtors are collected in 42 days. Creditors allow 32 days for payment. The length of the net operating cycle is:

options.B: 60 days
options.C: 70 days
options.D: 92 days

q: The annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 54,75,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. Its operating cycle is 60 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required by the enterprise is:

The working capital of an enterprise is estimated from the following components: raw material stock Rs 1,80,000, work-in-progress Rs 90,000, finished goods stock Rs 2,10,000, debtors Rs 3,00,000 and cash balance Rs 40,000, against which there are trade creditors of Rs 1,40,000 and outstanding expenses of Rs 30,000. The net working capital required is:
The net working capital of an enterprise is estimated at Rs 8,00,000. A margin of 10 per cent is added for contingencies. The total working capital to be provided for is:

The annual credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 36,50,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. Its customers take, on an average, 45 days to pay their dues. The amount of funds that will remain blocked in debtors is:

The annual consumption of a raw material in a factory is Rs 7,30,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. The factory wishes to hold raw material stock equal to 60 days' consumption. The value of the raw material stock to be held is:

The annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 29,20,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. Its suppliers allow, on an average, 30 days' credit. The amount that will remain owing to trade creditors is:

The projected sales of an enterprise for the coming year are Rs 48,00,000 and, on the percentage-of-sales method, its working capital is estimated at 25 per cent of the sales. The working capital requirement of the enterprise is:
The net sales of an enterprise for a year are Rs 42,00,000 and its average working capital during the year is Rs 7,00,000. Its working capital turnover ratio is:

options.B: 35 times
options.C: 6 times
options.D: 60 per cent

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 13,50,000 and its average inventory during the year is Rs 2,70,000. Its inventory turnover ratio is:

options.B: 0.20 times
options.C: 2.70 times
options.D: 50 times

q: The debtors of an enterprise stand at Rs 1,80,000 and its annual credit sales are Rs 10,95,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. Its average collection period is:

options.B: 365 days
options.C: 16 days
options.D: 60 days

q: The annual demand for a material is 16,000 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 25 and the carrying cost is Rs 5 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:

options.B: 400 units
options.C: 800 units
options.D: 4,000 units

q: An enterprise has an inventory conversion period of 55 days, a receivables collection period of 38 days and a payables deferral period of 33 days. Its cash conversion cycle is:

options.B: 93 days
options.C: 60 days
options.D: 22 days

q: Which of the following is a long-term source of finance, suitable for meeting the permanent part of the working capital of an enterprise?

options.A: Equity share capital and retained earnings of the enterprise
options.B: Trade credit obtained from the suppliers of materials
options.C: A cash credit limit repayable on demand
options.D: Outstanding wages and expenses awaiting payment

q: An enterprise holds bills receivable drawn on its customers, which will mature after two months, but it needs funds at once for its working capital. It can raise short-term funds against these bills by:

options.A: Issuing bonus shares to its shareholders
options.B: Selling its plant and machinery
options.C: Capitalising its general reserve
options.D: Discounting the bills with its bank, receiving the amount less the discount for the unexpired period

q: A dividend declared by the Board of Directors at a meeting held between two annual general meetings, before the accounts for the full year are closed, is a/an:

options.B: Interim dividend
options.C: Bonus dividend
options.D: Liquidating dividend

q: The dividend which is recommended by the Board of Directors and declared by the shareholders at the annual general meeting in respect of the full year is the:

options.B: Scrip dividend
options.C: Final dividend
options.D: Preference dividend

q: Instead of paying any cash, a company allots fully paid-up shares to its existing shareholders, free of cost and in proportion to their holdings, by capitalising a part of its reserves. Such a distribution of shares is a:

options.A: Stock dividend, in the form of bonus shares
options.B: Rights issue of shares for cash
options.C: Buy-back of its own shares by the company
options.D: Issue of shares to the public for the first time

q: A company subdivides each of its existing shares of Rs 100 into ten shares of Rs 10 each, the total paid-up share capital of the company remaining exactly the same. This action of the company is a:

options.B: Rights issue of shares
options.C: Buy-back of shares
options.D: Split (sub-division) of its shares

q: A company whose earnings fluctuate widely from year to year is generally cautious about raising its regular dividend to a high level in a good year, mainly because:

options.A: A high dividend in one year is prohibited in every case
options.B: A dividend level once raised creates an expectation of its continuance, and a cut in a later lean year is read by investors as a sign of weakness and may depress the price of the share
options.C: The dividend of a company must be the same in every year by law
options.D: Fluctuating earnings make it impossible to compute the dividend

q: Small investors who depend on the income from their shares for meeting their regular expenses generally prefer to hold the shares of companies which follow a:

options.A: Policy of paying no dividend in any year
options.B: Policy of paying the whole of the earnings as dividend every year
options.C: Stable dividend policy, paying a regular dividend that does not fluctuate sharply with the earnings of each year
options.D: Policy of changing the dividend with every small change in earnings

q: A young and growing company which has several profitable expansion opportunities before it, but only limited access to outside finance, will normally adopt:

options.A: A low dividend payout, retaining a large part of its earnings to finance its growth from within
options.B: A payout of the whole of its earnings as dividend every year
options.C: A policy of borrowing heavily in order to pay a high dividend
options.D: A policy of paying dividend out of its share capital

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A company may earn a large profit and yet be unable to pay a large cash dividend, if much of the profit is locked up in debtors and stock and its cash position is weak.
2. The payment of a cash dividend reduces the cash and, with it, the working capital of the company.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.B: 2 only
options.C: Neither 1 nor 2
options.D: Both 1 and 2

q: The profit after tax of a company for a year is Rs 9,00,000 and its dividend payout ratio is 40 per cent. The total amount distributed as dividend for the year is:
The Earnings Per Share of a company are Rs 22 and the Dividend Per Share declared is Rs 8. The earnings retained per share are:

options.B: Rs 8
options.C: Rs 14
options.D: Rs 22

q: The Earnings Per Share of a company are Rs 18 and its Dividend Per Share is Rs 6. Its dividend payout ratio is:

options.B: 300 per cent
options.C: 66.67 per cent
options.D: 18 per cent

q: The Dividend Per Share of a company is Rs 9 and the market price of its share is Rs 150. Its dividend yield is:

options.B: 150 per cent
options.C: 0.06 per cent
options.D: 6 per cent

q: The profit available for the equity shareholders of a company is Rs 8,80,000 and the equity dividend declared by it is Rs 2,20,000. Its dividend cover is:

options.B: 4 times
options.C: 25 per cent
options.D: 2.20 times

q: A company earns a return on equity of 18 per cent and its dividend payout ratio is 50 per cent. Its sustainable growth rate, computed as the return on equity multiplied by the retention ratio, is:

options.B: 18 per cent
options.C: 9 per cent
options.D: 36 per cent

q: Under Walter's model of dividend policy, where the return earned by the firm on its retained earnings (r) is lower than the rate of return required by the shareholders (ke), the market price of the share is the highest when the firm:

options.A: Pays out the whole of its earnings as dividend, since the shareholders can employ the money to better advantage than the firm can
options.B: Retains the whole of its earnings and pays no dividend at all
options.C: Retains exactly one-half of its earnings every year
options.D: Pays a dividend only once in five years

q: In Walter's model, the market price of a share is given by P = [D + (r/ke)(E - D)] / ke, where E is the earnings per share, D is the dividend per share, r is the return on investment and ke is the cost of equity. For a share with E = Rs 10, D = Rs 4, r = 15 per cent and ke = 10 per cent, the market price is:

options.B: Rs 90
options.C: Rs 115
options.D: Rs 130

q: Gordon's approach to the valuation of a share rests on valuing the share as:

options.A: The book value of the net assets backing the share
options.B: The present value of all the dividends expected to be received on the share in the future, discounted at the shareholders' required rate of return
options.C: The dividend declared in the latest year alone, without any discounting
options.D: The liquidation value of the assets of the company

q: The conclusion of the Modigliani-Miller approach that dividend policy does not affect the value of a firm rests, among others, on the assumption that:

options.A: The firm pays tax at a very high rate on its profits
options.B: The shares of the firm cannot be bought or sold in the market at all
options.C: There are no taxes and no costs of issuing new shares, and the investment programme of the firm is given and does not change with its dividend decision
options.D: The firm has no profitable investment opportunity before it

q: In value analysis, a component is said to suffer from poor value when:

options.A: Its cost is high in absolute terms, whatever function it performs
options.B: It has been in use for a long period without replacement
options.C: It is purchased from an outside supplier instead of being made in-house
options.D: The cost incurred on it is out of proportion to the usefulness of the function it performs

q:
Consider the following statements about value analysis:
1. It questions whether every feature and tolerance specified for a component is really necessary for the function required.
2. It seeks the cheapest way of performing the required function without sacrificing quality, reliability or appearance.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes value analysis from ordinary cost reduction?

options.A: Value analysis reduces cost by accepting a lower quality of the product, while cost reduction does not
options.B: Cost reduction works item by item on cost, while value analysis works function by function and asks what the item does before asking what it costs
options.C: Value analysis is applied only by the accounts department, while cost reduction is applied only by engineers
options.D: There is no difference between the two in either approach or result

q: In a value analysis study, the phase in which a large number of alternative ways of performing the same function are generated without judging them at that stage is the:

options.B: Evaluation phase
options.C: Recommendation phase
options.D: Creativity (speculation) phase

q: A value analysis team for a stores item is most appropriately composed of:

options.A: Officers of the accounts department alone
options.B: External consultants alone, without any departmental staff
options.C: Representatives of the suppliers of the item alone
options.D: A multi-disciplinary group drawn from design, production, purchase, costing and the user department concerned

q: In value engineering, the 'worth' of a function means:

options.A: The price at which the finished product is sold in the market
options.B: The total cost actually incurred in performing the function at present
options.C: The lowest cost at which the function can be performed reliably by any available alternative
options.D: The book value of the asset performing the function

q:
Consider the following statements about management audit:
1. It extends beyond the financial records to the plans, objectives, policies and organisational structure of the enterprise.
2. It is concerned only with verifying that the books of account give a true and fair view.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes management audit from operational audit?

options.A: Operational audit appraises the top management as a whole, while management audit examines only one operation
options.B: Management audit is a statutory requirement, while operational audit is voluntary
options.C: Operational audit examines the efficiency of a specific operation or function, while management audit appraises the quality of management and its decision-making more broadly
options.D: There is no difference between the two in scope or purpose

q: A management audit that stops at pointing out weaknesses, without examining the reasons behind them and suggesting the course of corrective action, fails in its purpose because management audit is essentially:

options.A: A fault-finding exercise over past transactions
options.B: A check on the arithmetical accuracy of the accounts
options.C: A substitute for the annual financial audit
options.D: A forward-looking and constructive appraisal intended to improve future performance

q: The effectiveness of a management audit depends most heavily on:

options.A: The number of vouchers checked during the audit
options.B: The competence, independence and objectivity of the team conducting it, and the support it receives from top management
options.C: The size of the audit department in relation to the total staff
options.D: The use of the same audit programme every year without change

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A management audit may cover the soundness of the enterprise's organisational structure and the clarity with which authority and responsibility are assigned.
2. A management audit is confined to examining whether expenditure was incurred with the sanction of the competent authority.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: A Management Information System (MIS) is best described as:

options.A: A set of registers in which the transactions of the enterprise are first recorded
options.B: A system for filing the correspondence received from higher offices
options.C: A computer programme used only for preparing the payroll
options.D: An organised system for collecting, processing, storing and supplying information in the right form, to the right person and at the right time for decision-making

q: At the strategic (top management) level, the information required is characteristically:

options.B: Confined to the records of a single section or shop
options.C: Highly summarised, largely forward-looking and drawn substantially from sources outside the enterprise as well as within it
options.D: Concerned only with correcting errors in the day-to-day postings

q:
Consider the following statements about reporting levels:
1. Information for operational (supervisory) control is detailed, frequent and mainly historical, relating to current operations.
2. Information for top management is detailed and frequent in the same manner as at the operational level.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes tactical (middle management) information from operational information?

options.A: Tactical information is concerned with the performance of departments over weeks and months and with the use of resources, while operational information is concerned with individual current transactions and tasks
options.B: Tactical information is always obtained from outside the enterprise, while operational information is never so obtained
options.C: Operational information covers a longer future period than tactical information
options.D: There is no difference between the two in scope, period or detail

q: Reporting by exception, as a principle of management reporting, means that:

options.A: Reports are prepared only in years in which an exception has been taken by audit
options.B: No report is sent to a manager unless his results are unsatisfactory
options.C: Normal and satisfactory performance is not burdened in the report; significant deviations from plan are highlighted for the manager's attention
options.D: Every transaction of the period is listed in full in the report to top management

q: A good management report should possess, among others, the qualities of:

options.A: Maximum detail, irrespective of the level to which it is sent
options.B: Preparation only after the annual accounts have been audited
options.C: Length sufficient to cover every account head operated in the period
options.D: Relevance to the recipient's responsibilities, promptness, accuracy sufficient for its purpose and a cost of preparation proportionate to its usefulness

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Under Current Cost Accounting (CCA), assets are shown in the balance sheet at their current replacement (value to the business) values.
2. Under Current Purchasing Power (CPP) accounting, historical costs are retained but are restated in units of equal purchasing power.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes CCA from CPP accounting?

options.A: CPP uses a specific price index for each asset, while CCA uses a single general price index
options.B: CCA measures the effect of changes in the specific prices of the enterprise's own assets, while CPP measures the effect of the change in the general price level on historical amounts
options.C: CCA ignores inflation altogether, while CPP is based on replacement cost
options.D: There is no difference between the two in the index or values used

q: In inflation accounting, 'monetary items' are items which:

options.A: Are held for resale in the ordinary course of business
options.B: Rise in value in the same proportion as the general price level
options.C: Represent money held, or claims to receive or obligations to pay a fixed number of rupees, regardless of changes in prices
options.D: Have no physical existence, such as goodwill

q: An asset was purchased for Rs 1,50,000 when the general price index stood at 150. At the balance sheet date the index stands at 225. Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method, the restated value of the asset is:
In a period of falling prices, under Current Purchasing Power (CPP) accounting, an enterprise holding net monetary assets (monetary assets exceeding its monetary liabilities) experiences:

options.A: A purchasing power gain, because the fixed money amounts it holds or is owed gain in purchasing power as prices fall
options.B: A purchasing power loss, because it must repay its liabilities in dearer money
options.C: Neither a gain nor a loss, because monetary items are never restated
options.D: A loss equal to the fall in the replacement cost of its fixed assets

q: Under Current Cost Accounting (CCA), the Depreciation Adjustment is made in order to:

options.A: Charge depreciation on the historical cost of the asset over its original estimated life only
options.B: Avoid charging depreciation altogether during inflation
options.C: Write off the asset in the year of purchase itself
options.D: Charge depreciation on the current cost of the asset, so that the higher amount needed to maintain operating capability is provided

q:
Consider the following statements about human resource accounting:
1. It treats expenditure on recruitment, training and development of employees as an investment rather than purely as a period expense.
2. It requires every employee to be shown in the balance sheet at his salary for the year.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the historical cost approach from the replacement cost approach to human resource accounting?

options.A: The historical cost approach values people at the cost of replacing them, while the replacement cost approach capitalises the cost actually incurred on them
options.B: The historical cost approach capitalises the actual cost incurred on acquiring and developing employees and amortises it over their expected service, while the replacement cost approach values them at the cost that would now be incurred to replace them with equivalent staff
options.C: Both approaches value employees at the present value of their future earnings
options.D: Neither approach places any monetary value on human resources

q: A recognised limitation of human resource accounting is that:

options.A: Employees can be valued with the same precision as plant and machinery
options.B: The ownership of human resources rests with the enterprise in the same way as physical assets
options.C: There is no generally accepted and objective method of valuing people, and employees are not owned by the enterprise, so the values remain largely subjective
options.D: Its results are prescribed in detail by an accounting standard in force

q: Under the Lev and Schwartz model, if the expected future earnings of an employee rise while the discount rate and the remaining service period remain unchanged, the computed value of that employee will:

options.A: Fall, because higher earnings mean a higher cost to the enterprise
options.B: Rise, because the present value of a larger stream of future earnings is higher
options.C: Remain unchanged, because the model does not use future earnings
options.D: Become nil, because the model applies only at the date of recruitment

q: Information from human resource accounting is most useful to management for:

options.A: Deciding the market price of the finished product
options.B: Fixing the rate of depreciation on plant and machinery
options.C: Computing the break-even point of the enterprise
options.D: Decisions on manpower planning, training investment and the return obtained on the expenditure incurred on developing employees

q:
Consider the following statements about Activity-Based Management (ABM):
1. It uses activity cost information to decide which activities add value and which do not.
2. It is concerned only with assigning overhead costs to products more accurately, and not with improving the activities themselves.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: An activity for which the customer is willing to pay, and without which the product or service cannot be provided as required, is classified in activity-based management as:

options.A: A non-value-added activity, to be eliminated at once
options.B: A waste activity, to be charged to the profit and loss account
options.C: A facility-sustaining activity, to be ignored in analysis
options.D: A value-added activity, to be performed as efficiently as possible

q: Repeated inspection of the same component, movement of material between shops solely due to poor layout, and waiting time of machines for material are, in activity-based management, examples of:

options.A: Value-added activities which must be increased
options.B: Non-value-added activities, whose cost is a prime target for elimination or reduction without affecting the product
options.C: Product-sustaining activities which cannot be examined
options.D: Activities whose cost must be spread over all products equally

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes activity-based management from activity-based costing?

options.D: There is no difference between the two in purpose or use

q:
Consider the following statements about target costing:

q: Target costing is most effective for a product whose selling price is:

q:
Consider the following statements about kaizen costing:

options.B: 2 only

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes kaizen costing from target costing?

options.A: Target costing operates during production, while kaizen costing operates only at the design stage

q: A kaizen cost-reduction target is most appropriately set and pursued as:
